s: Low-gravity letter romp, playable
why: A whole mini game designed from our identity; waiting on your go to build it.

s: The study: map, town, front, inside
why: Decides what Abbie’s café is at every distance before anything is built.

s: Locked back bar; five pieces in three styles
why: Picks the model style for every café piece.

s: Every item in your pick, floors and walls
why: The list every café model is built from.

s: 48 pictures by view and style
why: You picked the dance-party room from these.

s: The normal human: proportions, muscles, scorecard
why: The canon of a normal human body every figure is measured against.

s: Paper bodies from your picks, in 3D
why: Body types the Roman kit and every later figure stand on.

s: Your reference man, part by part: helmet, cuirass, shoulders, belt, gladius, sandals
why: Parts-first modelling of one exact figure, each piece beside its picture.

s: Six ways to split one brute, scored from the same camera
why: Finds the way of splitting a model across jobs that gets one exact figure right.

s: The tour guide, three welcomes, the 30-second tour
why: How every new player meets the game, and the list of stops every new feature can join.

s: One exact heroic figure, built the way the bruiser taught us
why: Applies the bruiser method to a second figure: turnaround, depth ruler, anatomy base, planes.

s: The office under the café: her 1986 computer, playable
why: The first room you play from the side, with a working computer, disks and ten coins to find.

s: Climb the old school at dusk, sneak the roof, 31 balls for the dog
why: A spoken memory became a playable game in one sitting: first-person climb, iso roof, a hang-drop and a gold memory coin.

s: Two painted Meshy brutes brawl in a ranch ring: jab, heavy, uppercut, hammer
why: The first fighting game: Meshy heroes cleaned up, painted, rigged on one skeleton, 19 moves with a hit and a blocked reaction for every blow.

s: Can three.js paint the soft clay animated-film look? Live, part by part
why: Shows the film look runs live in the browser: eight switchable shader parts beside your picture.

s: Faceted Hero look and the 40-body base roster: shapes, sizes, races, aliens
why: One faceted body set, PG and true to shape, that every hero and the gear kit fit.

s: Everyone in Daddy's memory places, then and now, with designed voices to pick
why: One shared cast for every memory game: a storybook sheet and a designed voice per person, so the school, the basement and the Moon base all sound like the same family.

s: 200 low-poly pieces for the Moon shooter, 20 built with baked maps and mass
why: The world the low-gravity shooter walks through: named parts, real materials baked to colour, roughness and normal maps, mass per part, and diegetic gauges and lamps instead of a HUD.

s: One tap moves the right hand; a new school, bub the black lab and young Daddy at golden dusk
why: The school jump made game ready: the climb fixed, a full UX pass, and every model rebuilt as a hero low-poly recipe that the next memory game can reuse.

s: A headland chosen by simulation; the tile splits into 217 hex blocks and a town grows
why: A city-builder version of Abbie's World: water by gravity, goods chains, four kinds of household and townspeople who talk, all from the land up.

s: Young Daddy, bub and the basement girl rebuilt so the storybook light has form to work on
why: The memory-place figures were stacks of primitives; now each is a few skinned surfaces with cloth, hair and fur, so rim light, glowing ears and the pixel pass read as a character.

s: How RSI, Starfield and EVE design ships, the Oracle's 27 space games, and the rules our Aurora Mk 2 follows
why: Before building a ship we studied how the great space games build theirs: silhouette, modules, boarding, cockpit, flight feel. The Mk 2 brief comes from those findings.

s: Family couch game for the big TV: pink rocket, launch morning, live Houston, lander to the Moon base
why: Tonight after ballet: Daddy, Abbie and Ani fly to the Moon base together, each with an important job.

s: The wooden mannequin rigged and moving: 50 moves from 11 game genres, on the mannequin and the Meshy brutes
why: One skeleton and one way of writing poses for every body, so a move made once plays on the mannequin, the Meshy brutes and the heroes to come. The 2D puppet is its second tab.

s: The blue-graphite wooden mannequin as a 2D toy: drag its joints, set keys, play 18 moves
why: The 2D side of the Character Studio: the practice mannequin rigged with drag-to-pose joints, a key strip and stock moves sorted by game genre, on the studio's shared bone names.

s: 18 feelings on a 3D toy, a painted face and a faceless body; a typed line drives the face
why: How your games do faces, turned into one expression set every character can use, driven by the voice and the line.

s: Dress the rigged Meshy brutes in four looks, paint them part by part, watch them walk
why: One studio where any rigged hero wears any art direction (whimsical clay, Stick Man storybook, Wallace and Gromit plasticine, 80s cartoon action) with named-part paint, bump and our shaders, walking from a distance.

s: The mannequin in SVG pieces on bones: IK arms you can pull, a walk, and a jump with real squash and stretch
why: Characters drawn professionally in pieces, rigged the way Spine and Rive games are, in a format the 2D puppet and the Character Studio share. Six practice reps, creative score 4 to 19 of 24.

s: A charming town on the real land of Winchester, MA at true scale, with Evan's places and an asset manifest to the soccer ball
why: Abbie's own town: her coffee shop, Muraco and the fields, with Daddy's childhood places and coins inside it.

s: Moon astronauts in plasticine and painterly looks, then 40 PG base bodies and the story heroes
why: Every hero character made in Meshy, cleaned up, geared and rigged, shown in one place.

s: A Midjourney sketch traced four ways, and a puppet that keeps its line when it moves
why: Why code-drawn figures look weak next to Midjourney: we redraw instead of trace, never measure, and score only silhouettes. Proven on the 2D mannequin.

s: Fourteen modern game looks rebuilt live on our models, with the Arcane-inspired Painted Brush; pick the ones you love
why: Chooses the game's toon set: each look is one shared material driven by one game signal (time of day, wind, music), and Painted Brush is already a kit for the heroes.

s: Say it, Midjourney for the feel, pose the mannequin, then a code pencil draws the lines
why: Evan's perfect-world drawing chain tried end to end, with an emulated graphite pencil and an even-better-if loop per attempt.

s: Every inventory is a backpack: it opens half shell, ten styles, five facets, and a charm for every quest
why: Game canon: the one player inventory becomes a backpack she dresses up, and quests now pay out in charms tied to Daddy's core memories.

s: A woman and a man, posed in 3D and drawn with the code pencil, in a leap and a run
why: The pose drives the pencil drawing for the first time: sealed mannequin bodies, line render, then pencil with form hatching. PG base layers.

s: The green goo by the science lab is alive: a top-down single-cell battler in SVG, seen through a liquid-glass lens
why: Our first 2D game: shader water, rigged SVG cells and the lens on every body. The microbe kit and lens pond are shared for the next 2D game.

s: The pasted flying hero cut into parts on a named skeleton, with a Unity-style export
why: A picture becomes a rigged cut-out: 16 parts, 3 decorations, 16 bones, posable, with a Unity builder script (untested in Unity).

s: How you switch which board is shown and make new ones (zoom out to the board of boards), plus doors and rides between places and the seven-hex Winchester layout. Playable prototypes
why: Many boards, not one: switch, start new, name and keep them. Travel between places is a section.

s: A card that rains paint from the sky onto the board; it stays a day of game time and strange alien plants grow from it. Playable
why: Splatoon's paint-is-the-play idea as a gentle card: shader ink, sky drops and five low-poly alien plants driven by the game day clock.

s: The far world turns to wet watercolour, per Winchester zone: soft edges that bleed, flat washes, paper grain. A production shader live in the town dioramas
why: Pulling back feels like stepping away from a painting, and each region has its own colours.

s: Poses held for two film frames, a pen line redrawn every drawing, paper grain: a switch for any figure, live in the brute fight
why: Limited animation (Guilty Gear Xrd) as a production look: held frames make hits read heavy, and it costs no extra shader programs.

s: Fourteen modern lighting looks rebuilt live on our ranch, Winchester, café, basement, Moon base and a playful Halloween; pick the ones you love
why: Chooses how light feels in the game: one time-of-day signal drives sun, sky, fog, lamps and window glow together, with looks for the Winchester day, the café, the basement, the Moon base and Halloween.

s: Where can I earn my charms? A chest of ten, locked cards with a padlock where they unlock, a jewellery box with glass domes, and the mission board, on the seven-hex Winchester board
why: Sets how charms are found and kept (chest, locked cards, jewellery box) and the mission board style the demo builds.

s: A 30 second first-person ride on an orange toy-car coaster built in the skate park by the school: loop, hills, corkscrew, a gap jump, boosters, sixteen stars and a charm. Tile view flows down to a tilt-shift track, then you get in the car
why: First ride-style minigame: a track is a recipe of straights, turns, pitches and rolls, so loops and jumps become numbers. Adds the toy-car charm and the tilt-shift miniature view.

t: The Effect Hunt and the Jet Cart
s: Ten collectible world effects hidden around Winchester, laser beacons, and a jetpack shopping cart carrying Abbie, Ani and Daddy. Kart and overhead modes, a friendly critter tows you home. Playable
why: Gives the board a reason to roam: a hunt with a feel of its own, built from the Paint the World recipe.

s: The board becomes a looping racetrack stencilled from its tiles and rebuilt in the background when a tile is placed. Crash into scenery, ramps, boost pads, laps. Playable
why: Makes driving a game of its own and gives every new tile a job.

s: A four-minute minigame in six stations, a glass-sided tunnel you can see out of, and an original disco-funk song with a section for each station. Drafted: the plan, not yet built.
why: Turns a five-second drive-through into a game you replay for stars.

s: Choose a family, season, land and how alive; the game decorates a first pass; then you build freely. Weather, physics and gravity wait behind a flask. Experimental: open with ?exp=scene-builder.
why: A first-class in-game lab for building and experimenting with whole worlds.
